debounce.desc: A classic that interviewers love. Delay execution until the user stops triggering the event.
debounce.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement debounce(fn, delay)
debounce.what:
Implement a debounce(fn, delay) function. The function it returns should call fn only after delay milliseconds have passed since the last call. It should also expose a .cancel() method that discards any pending invocation.

Requirements

  • Basic debounce: run fn only after a quiet period
  • Return a wrapper that forwards the same arguments to fn
  • Add a .cancel() method that clears the pending timer
  • Preserve the correct this context inside fn
  • Leading-edge option: fire immediately on the first call when { leading: true } is passed

Concepts: closures · timers · higher-order functions · this binding
debounce.why:
• Use setTimeout and clearTimeout. Keep the timer ID in a variable that the closure can reach.
  • For the leading edge: call fn immediately if no timer is running, then start a timer that marks when the next leading call is allowed.

throttle.desc: Limits how often a function can fire. It is debounce's sibling and is often confused with it.
throttle.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement throttle(fn, delay)
throttle.what:
Implement throttle(fn, delay). The function it returns should call fn at most once every delay ms, no matter how often it is invoked. Support both leading and trailing calls.

Requirements

  • Basic throttle: call fn at most once per delay window
  • Leading call: fire immediately on the first invocation
  • Trailing call: if the function is called during a window, fire once when the window ends
  • Return a wrapper that forwards the same arguments to fn
  • Provide a cancel method that clears a pending trailing call

Concepts: closures · timers · rate limiting · higher-order functions
throttle.why:
• Track a lastCalled timestamp. On each call, check whether (now - lastCalled) >= delay. If so, call fn and update lastCalled.
  • For the trailing call: save the latest arguments in the closure and use setTimeout to call fn when the remaining time in the window runs out.

curry.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement curry(fn)
curry.what:
Write curry(fn), which returns a curried version of fn. The curried function accepts arguments one at a time and calls fn only once all of them have been collected. It should also support partial application, where several arguments are passed at once.

Requirements

  • Works for functions of any arity (fn.length)
  • Accepts arguments one at a time: add(1)(2)(3)
  • Supports partial application: add(1,2)(3)
  • Returns the result as soon as all arguments are collected
  • Handles functions with default parameters (the fn.length caveat)

Concepts: closures · recursion · function.length · partial application

memoize.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement memoize(fn)
memoize.what:
Implement memoize(fn), which returns a memoized version of fn that caches results by arguments. Support an optional resolver function to compute the cache key. Also expose a .cache property and a .clear() method.

Requirements

  • By default, use JSON.stringify(args) as the cache key
  • Support an optional resolver(...args) that computes a custom cache key
  • Expose the cache Map on the returned function as .cache
  • Add a .clear() method that empties the cache
  • Handle object arguments correctly (key serialization)

Concepts: closures · Map · JSON.stringify · higher-order functions
memoize.why:
• Keep a Map in the closure. Key = resolver ? resolver(...args) : JSON.stringify(args). Check the map before calling fn.
  • JSON.stringify has limits: it drops undefined and Symbol values and throws on circular references. Mention this as a trade-off.

pipe-compose.desc: Function composition, the backbone of functional programming in JS.
pipe-compose.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement pipe() and compose()
pipe-compose.why:
• pipe = (...fns) => x => fns.reduce((v, f) => f(v), x). compose is the same idea, but uses reduceRight.
  • pipeAsync: use fns.reduce((promise, fn) => promise.then(fn), Promise.resolve(x))

flatten.q: How will you solve this problem? Flatten a Nested Array
flatten.what:
Implement flatten(arr, depth = Infinity), which behaves like Array.prototype.flat(). It flattens nested arrays up to the given depth. For bonus points, also write an iterative version that uses a stack.

Requirements

  • Handles any level of nesting
  • Respects the depth parameter (flatten(arr, 1) flattens only one level)
  • Does not modify the original array
  • Works with mixed types (numbers, strings, nested arrays)
  • Bonus: an iterative, stack-based solution

Concepts: recursion · Array.isArray · spread operator · stack

deep-clone.q: How will you solve this problem? Deep Clone an Object
deep-clone.why:
• Use a WeakMap to track objects you have already visited. Before cloning an object, check the map; if it is there, return the existing clone. This handles circular references.
  • Check types in this order: null → array → Date → RegExp → Map → Set → plain object.

once.desc: Run a function exactly once, then return the same value on every later call.
once.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement once(fn)
once.what:
Implement once(fn), which returns a wrapper that calls fn at most once. Every later call returns the result of the first call without invoking fn again.

Requirements

  • fn runs only on the first call
  • Later calls return the same cached result
  • Preserves fn's this context on the first call
  • Works with any number of arguments
  • Bonus: a .reset() method that clears the internal state

Concepts: closures · flag variables · this binding
once.why:
• Keep a boolean flag and a cached result variable in the closure.
  • let called = false, result; return function(...args){ if(!called){ called=true; result=fn.apply(this,args); } return result; }
  • For .reset(): set called=false and result=undefined, so fn can run again on the next call.

groupby.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement groupBy(array, key)
groupby.why: • Use reduce with {} as the accumulator. Compute the key with typeof key === "function" ? key(item) : item[key], then push the item into acc[k] = acc[k] || [];

array-methods.desc: Can you recreate the Array prototype methods? This tests your grasp of callbacks and accumulators.
array-methods.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement map / filter / reduce from Scratch
array-methods.what:
Implement myMap(arr, fn), myFilter(arr, fn), and myReduce(arr, fn, initialValue) without using the built-in methods. Each should match the native behavior, including edge cases.

Requirements

  • myMap: applies fn(item, index, array) to each element
  • myFilter: returns a new array of the elements for which fn returns a truthy value
  • myReduce: when there is no initialValue, uses the first element as the accumulator
  • All three pass the index and the original array to the callback
  • Throw a TypeError when the callback is not a function (as the native methods do)

Concepts: callbacks · accumulators · array iteration · prototype methods

bind.desc: The mother of all polyfills. It tests this binding, partial application, and the new operator trap.
bind.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement Function.prototype.bind
bind.what:
Implement Function.prototype.bind(thisArg, ...partials). It returns a new function whose this is fixed to thisArg and which prepends partials to the call arguments. The tricky part: when the bound function is called with new, the bound this is ignored and the newly created instance takes precedence.

Requirements

  • Returns a new function that calls the original with a fixed this
  • Supports partial application: bind(ctx, a, b)(c, d) → fn.call(ctx, a, b, c, d)
  • When used as a constructor (new), the bound this is ignored
  • The bound function keeps the original prototype so instanceof checks work
  • Handles a missing thisArg (defaults to globalThis in sloppy mode)

Concepts: this binding · partial application · new operator · prototype chain
bind.why:
• Keep fn and thisArg in the closure. Return a wrapper that merges boundArgs with the call-time args.
  • For the new trap: use instanceof to detect whether the wrapper was called with new. If it was, return new original(...mergedArgs) instead of fn.apply(thisArg, mergedArgs).

object-assign.desc: Merging objects is everywhere. Implement it per the spec, including getter invocation.
object-assign.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement Object.assign
object-assign.what:
Implement Object.assign(target, ...sources). Copy own enumerable properties from each source to the target, using [[Get]] on the source and [[Set]] on the target. Return the target. (A basic version handles string keys; the full spec also copies Symbol keys.)

Requirements

  • Copies own enumerable properties only (a basic version handles string keys; the spec also copies Symbols)
  • Uses [[Get]] on the source (invokes getters) and [[Set]] on the target
  • Later sources overwrite earlier ones
  • Null and undefined sources are skipped without error
  • Primitive sources are coerced to objects
  • Returns the modified target object

Concepts: Object.keys · property descriptors · for...in vs own properties
object-assign.why:
• Loop over the sources with forEach. For each one, take Object.keys(source) and assign target[key] = source[key] for every key.
  • The subtlety: reading source[key] invokes getters, which is what the spec requires. Do NOT copy the property descriptor (getOwnPropertyDescriptor) or the getter itself.

array-from.desc: The most versatile Array static method. It handles iterables, array-likes, and a map function.
array-from.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement Array.from

array-find.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement Array.prototype.find
array-find.what:
Implement Array.prototype.find(callback, thisArg?). It returns the first element that satisfies the callback, or undefined if none does. Handle sparse arrays correctly.

Requirements

  • Returns the first element for which the callback returns a truthy value
  • Returns undefined if no element matches
  • The callback receives (element, index, array)
  • An optional thisArg sets this inside the callback
  • Visits empty slots in sparse arrays as undefined (unlike map and filter, find does not skip them)
  • Does not mutate the original array

Concepts: array iteration · early termination · sparse arrays · this binding

array-includes.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement Array.prototype.includes

string-methods.desc: Three string methods with subtle spec details: position handling and the RegExp guard.
string-methods.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement String.prototype.startsWith / endsWith / includes
string-methods.why:
• startsWith: position = Math.min(Math.max(pos, 0), this.length). Slice from position to position+len, then compare.
  • The RegExp guard: if (searchString instanceof RegExp) throw new TypeError(). The spec requires this.

object-create.desc: The foundation of ES5 prototypal inheritance. Set up [[Prototype]] without the built-in.
object-create.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement Object.create
object-create.what:
Implement Object.create(proto, propertiesObject?). It creates a new object whose [[Prototype]] is proto. The optional second argument adds property descriptors (like Object.defineProperties).

Requirements

  • Returns a new object with [[Prototype]] set to proto
  • If proto is null, creates an object with no prototype
  • If proto is neither an object nor null, throws a TypeError
  • An optional propertiesObject defines own properties via Object.defineProperties
  • Common use: Child.prototype = Object.create(Parent.prototype)
  • Handles proto === null (no prototype chain)

Concepts: prototypal inheritance · Object.defineProperties · null prototype · constructor
object-create.why:
• The temporary-constructor trick: function F(){}; F.prototype = proto; return new F(). It works for any proto except null.
  • For null: use Object.setPrototypeOf({}, null), which gives an object with no prototype.

some-every.desc: The logical quantifiers: early-terminating iteration with vacuous-truth semantics.
some-every.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement Array.prototype.some and every

array-map.desc: The most-used array method. Implement the full spec, including sparse arrays and thisArg.
array-map.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement Array.prototype.map
array-map.what:
Implement Array.prototype.map(callback, thisArg?) on the Array prototype. It creates a new array filled with the results of calling callback on every element. Handle sparse arrays correctly: empty slots must stay empty in the result.

Requirements

  • Returns a new array (does not mutate the original)
  • The callback receives (element, index, array)
  • An optional thisArg sets this inside the callback
  • Skips empty slots in sparse arrays (the callback is not called and the slot stays empty)
  • Throws a TypeError if the callback is not a function
  • Works on array-like objects, not just Array instances

Concepts: prototype methods · array iteration · sparse arrays · this binding
array-map.why:
• Use a standard for loop. Check i in array to handle sparse arrays. For each existing slot: result[i] = callback.call(thisArg, array[i], i, array).
  • The key spec detail: map leaves a hole in the output for every hole in the input. It does not fill sparse slots with undefined.

array-filter.desc: The real test is sparse arrays: filter always skips holes.
array-filter.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement Array.prototype.filter
array-filter.what:
Implement Array.prototype.filter(callback, thisArg?). It returns a new array containing only the elements for which callback returns a truthy value. Unlike map, filter naturally compacts sparse arrays, so its result never has holes.

Requirements

  • Returns a new array (does not mutate the original)
  • The callback receives (element, index, array)
  • An optional thisArg sets this inside the callback
  • Skips empty slots in sparse arrays
  • Throws a TypeError if the callback is not a function
  • The result is always dense (no holes), with elements packed to the left

Concepts: prototype methods · array iteration · sparse arrays · truthiness
array-filter.why:
• Loop with an i in array check. If the callback returns a truthy value, push the element onto the result. Because push() appends sequentially, the result is always dense.
  • This sparse-to-dense behavior is what sets filter apart: map preserves holes, while filter removes them.

array-reduce.desc: The subtlest of the trio. The trap is a missing initialValue on an empty array.
array-reduce.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement Array.prototype.reduce
array-reduce.what:
Implement Array.prototype.reduce(callback, initialValue?). It runs a reducer function over each element and produces a single output value. If there is no initialValue, it uses the first element as the accumulator and starts from index 1.

Requirements

  • The callback receives (accumulator, element, index, array)
  • If initialValue is provided, acc = initialValue and the loop starts at index 0
  • If there is no initialValue, acc = first element and the loop starts at index 1
  • Throws a TypeError on an empty array with no initialValue
  • Throws a TypeError if the callback is not a function
  • Skips empty slots in sparse arrays (they are not counted)

Concepts: accumulators · edge cases · sparse arrays · TypeError
array-reduce.why:
• Do not test initialValue === undefined or truthiness: 0, "" and even undefined can be valid initial values. Use arguments.length < 2 to detect a missing initialValue.
  • With no initialValue: find the first non-hole index. If there is none (an empty array), throw a TypeError. Use that element as the initial acc and start the loop at index+1.

array-flat-flatmap.desc: flat, and map-then-flatten. flatMap is map followed by flat(1), and product companies ask about it a lot.
array-flat-flatmap.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement Array.prototype.flat and flatMap
array-flat-flatmap.what:
Implement Array.prototype.flat(depth = 1) and Array.prototype.flatMap(callback, thisArg?). flat recursively flattens nested arrays up to depth. flatMap is equivalent to map().flat(1): it flattens only one level.

Requirements

  • flat(depth): recursively flattens nested arrays up to the given depth (default 1)
  • flat(Infinity) flattens completely
  • flat drops empty slots from the flattened result
  • flatMap: maps each element, then flattens the result by one level
  • flatMap behaves like map followed by flat(1), but does it in a single pass without building an intermediate array
  • Both return new arrays and never mutate the original

Concepts: recursion · flattening · prototype methods · flatMap as map + flatten
array-flat-flatmap.why:
• flat: iterate with a for loop. If the element is an array and depth > 0, recurse with depth-1 and push each result. Otherwise push the element directly. Holes are dropped naturally.
  • flatMap: call the callback on each element, which should return an array. Use result.push(...callback(item, i, arr)) to flatten one level. This is equivalent to [].concat(...arr.map(callback)).

call-apply.desc: The foundation of explicit this binding. Implement the methods that bind, call, and apply build on.
call-apply.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement Function.prototype.call and apply
call-apply.what:
Implement Function.prototype.call(thisArg, ...args) and Function.prototype.apply(thisArg, argsArray). Both invoke the function with a specific this value. call takes arguments individually, while apply takes an array. Handle the edge cases: a null or undefined thisArg defaults to globalThis, and a non-function caller throws a TypeError.

Requirements

  • call: invokes the function with thisArg and individual arguments
  • apply: invokes the function with thisArg and the arguments as an array
  • null or undefined thisArg → default to globalThis (window/global) in sloppy mode
  • Throw a TypeError if the caller is not a function
  • apply: if argsArray is null or undefined, treat it as an empty array
  • Handle primitive thisArg values (box them with Object())

Concepts: this binding · globalThis · function methods · type checking

string-trim.desc: It looks trivial, but the spec defines whitespace broadly and you must handle both ends.
string-trim.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement String.prototype.trim
string-trim.what:
Implement String.prototype.trim(), trimStart(), and trimEnd(). They remove whitespace from both ends (trim), the start (trimStart), or the end (trimEnd). Whitespace includes space, tab, no-break space, line terminators (\n, \r, \f, \v), and all Unicode whitespace.

Requirements

  • trim(): removes whitespace from both ends
  • trimStart(): removes whitespace from the start only
  • trimEnd(): removes whitespace from the end only
  • Define whitespace: space, tab, no-break space, line terminators
  • If the string is all whitespace, return an empty string
  • Does not mutate the original string (strings are immutable)

Concepts: string methods · whitespace definition · regular expressions · immutability

array-sort.desc: The most complex Array prototype method. Implement the default string sort and comparator support.
array-sort.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement Array.prototype.sort (basic)
array-sort.what:
Implement Array.prototype.sort(compareFn?). The default sort converts elements to strings and compares their UTF-16 code units. If compareFn is provided, sort uses it: a negative result means a comes first, a positive result means b comes first, and zero means they are equal. Sort in place and return the same array.

Requirements

  • Default sort: converts elements to strings and compares UTF-16 code unit values
  • compareFn: (a, b) => negative (a first), positive (b first), zero (keep order)
  • Sorts in place and returns the modified array
  • Handles sparse arrays (empty slots are moved to the end)
  • Stable sort: equal elements keep their original relative order
  • Throws a TypeError if compareFn is provided but is not a function

Concepts: comparators · in-place sorting · string coercion · stable sort · sparse arrays
array-sort.why:
• Implement a simple stable sort such as insertion sort or merge sort. Insertion sort is O(n²) but stable and in place: for i=1..n-1, insert arr[i] into the sorted portion [0..i-1].
  • Default comparator: (a, b) => String(a) < String(b) ? -1 : String(a) > String(b) ? 1 : 0. For sparse arrays, record the holes and append them at the end.

promise-static.desc: The simplest Promise static methods, but thenable unwrapping in resolve is the hidden detail.
promise-static.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement Promise.resolve and Promise.reject
promise-static.what:
Implement Promise.resolve(value) and Promise.reject(reason). resolve returns a Promise resolved with the value, unwrapping thenables. reject returns a Promise rejected with the reason.

Requirements

  • Promise.resolve(value): returns a fulfilled Promise with the value
  • If the value is already a Promise, return it as is (no wrapping)
  • If the value is a thenable (has a .then method), unwrap it by calling value.then(resolve, reject)
  • Promise.reject(reason): returns a Promise rejected with the reason
  • reject does NOT unwrap thenables; it uses the value as the rejection reason as is
  • Both are static methods on Promise, not on instances

Concepts: Promise · thenable detection · static methods · unwrap semantics

reduce-right.desc: Like reduce, but from the right. The symmetry shows whether you really understand the accumulator pattern.
reduce-right.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement Array.prototype.reduceRight
reduce-right.what:
Implement Array.prototype.reduceRight(callback, initialValue?). It works like reduce but iterates from right to left, from the last element to the first. If there is no initialValue, the last element becomes the accumulator and iteration starts from the second-to-last.

Requirements

  • Iterates from the rightmost element to the leftmost
  • The callback receives (accumulator, element, index, array)
  • If initialValue is provided, acc = initialValue and the loop runs from the last index down to 0
  • If there is no initialValue, acc = last element and the loop runs from length-2 down to 0
  • Throws a TypeError on an empty array with no initialValue
  • Skips empty slots in sparse arrays

Concepts: accumulator pattern · right-to-left iteration · sparse arrays · TypeError
reduce-right.why:
• The logic is the same as reduce, but the loop runs backward: for (let i = len-1; i >= 0; i--). Check i in array for sparse support.
  • With no initialValue: find the last non-hole index, starting from the end. Use that element as acc and continue the loop from i-1 going backward.

eventemitter.desc: The backbone of Node.js. Building it from scratch is a top-5 machine coding question.
eventemitter.q: How will you solve this problem? Build EventEmitter (on/off/emit/once)
eventemitter.why:
• Store listeners in a Map: event → Set of listeners. For once, wrap the listener in a function that calls off first and then the original listener.
  • For off: Map.get(event)?.delete(listener). For once: create a oneTime wrapper and call on(event, oneTime). Inside oneTime, call off(event, oneTime) and then listener(...args).

lru.desc: O(1) get and put. A classic data structure question dressed up as machine coding.
lru.q: How will you solve this problem? LRU Cache with O(1) get and put
lru.what:
Implement an LRUCache(capacity) class. get(key) returns the value or -1, and put(key, value) inserts or updates an entry and evicts the least-recently-used item when capacity is exceeded.

Requirements

  • get(key): O(1). Return the value, or -1 if not found, and mark the key as recently used
  • put(key, value): O(1). Insert or update, and evict the LRU entry if over capacity
  • Both operations count as a "use" (they update recency)
  • Handle the capacity = 1 edge case
  • Bonus: implement it with a doubly linked list + Map (show the internals)

Concepts: Map (insertion-order) · doubly linked list · O(1) operations · hash map
lru.why:
• Use a Map, which preserves insertion order. To mark a key as recently used: delete(key), then set(key, value). To evict the LRU entry: map.keys().next().value gives the oldest key.
  • For the doubly-linked-list approach: the Map stores key → node, and the list maintains the order. On access, remove the node from the list and move it to the head. On eviction, remove the tail.

promise-scratch.desc: The deepest internals question. It shows that you truly understand async JavaScript.
promise-scratch.q: How will you solve this problem? Build Promise from Scratch

promise-combinators.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement Promise.all / race / allSettled / any
promise-combinators.what:
Implement Promise.all(promises), Promise.race(promises), Promise.allSettled(promises), and Promise.any(promises) from scratch, using only the base Promise constructor.

Requirements

  • all: resolves with an array of values; rejects on the first rejection
  • race: settles with the first promise to settle
  • allSettled: always resolves with an array of {status, value|reason}
  • any: resolves with the first fulfilled value; rejects with an AggregateError if all reject
  • All four handle empty arrays correctly
  • Preserve result order regardless of resolution order (for .all)

Concepts: Promise · counter pattern · AggregateError · async coordination

concurrency-limiter.q: How will you solve this problem? Async Concurrency Limiter
concurrency-limiter.what:
Implement runWithConcurrency(tasks, limit), where tasks is an array of functions that return Promises. Run at most limit tasks at the same time. Return a Promise that resolves with all results in the original order.

Requirements

  • At most limit tasks running at any time
  • The results array preserves the original task order
  • Starts the next task as soon as any running task completes
  • Returns a Promise that resolves with all results
  • Handles task rejections (reject the outer Promise)

Concepts: Promise · queue · async/await · worker pool
concurrency-limiter.why:
• Keep an index into the tasks array. Start limit tasks at first. When any task completes, start the next one from the queue. You can use Promise.race or a "worker" pattern.
  • Worker pattern: create limit worker Promises. Each worker pulls a task from the queue and awaits it, then pulls again, until the queue is empty. Wait for all of them with Promise.all(workers).

deep-equal.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement deepEqual(a, b)

retry.q: How will you solve this problem? Retry with Exponential Backoff
retry.what:
Implement retry(fn, retries, delay). Call the async fn. If it rejects, wait delay ms and try again, doubling the delay on each attempt (exponential backoff). After retries attempts, reject with the last error. Support a shouldRetry(error) predicate.

Requirements

  • Retry up to retries times on failure
  • Exponential backoff: the delay doubles each attempt (delay * 2^attempt)
  • Optional shouldRetry(err): if it returns false, stop retrying immediately
  • Resolve with fn's return value on success
  • Reject with the last error after all retries are exhausted

Concepts: async/await · recursion · exponential backoff · error handling
retry.why:
• Use a recursive async function with an attempt counter. Catch the error, check shouldRetry, then await sleep(delay * 2**attempt) before recursing.
  • sleep = ms => new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, ms))

chainable.q: How will you solve this problem? Build a Chainable Query Builder
chainable.why:
• Store an array of {method, fn} objects. value() runs them in sequence using the matching array method.
  • Return this from each method. Store operations as {type:"filter", fn} and reduce over them in value().

promise-timeout.q: How will you solve this problem? Implement withTimeout (Promise with a Timeout)
promise-timeout.what:
Implement withTimeout(promise, ms, fallback), which returns a new Promise that rejects with a TimeoutError (or resolves with a fallback) if the input promise does not settle within ms milliseconds. Build it on Promise.race. Also implement a sleep(ms) helper.

Requirements

  • withTimeout(p, ms) rejects with a TimeoutError if p takes longer than ms
  • If p settles first, its result or error passes through unchanged
  • No leaks: the losing branch of the race is observed, so there is no unhandled rejection
  • Support a fallback value (or function) that is used instead of rejecting on timeout
  • The timer is cleared once the promise settles (no dangling timers)
  • A sleep(ms) helper built on setTimeout

Concepts: Promise.race · setTimeout · timeout · unhandled rejection prevention
promise-timeout.why:
• withTimeout = (p, ms, fb) => Promise.race([p, sleep(ms).then(() => fb instanceof Function ? fb() : fb)]). This races the input against a timer that resolves to the fallback.
  • To avoid unhandled rejections on the losing branch, attach a no-op .catch(() => {}) to both promises before racing.

circuit-breaker.desc: The resilience pattern used at Atlassian and in nearly every backend service: fail fast instead of hanging on a dead dependency.
circuit-breaker.q: How will you solve this problem? Circuit Breaker (Fail Fast)
circuit-breaker.why:
• Store {state, failures, cooldownUntil}. On an error in CLOSED: increment failures; when it reaches the threshold, switch to OPEN and record cooldownUntil = now + cooldownPeriod.
  • While HALF_OPEN, allow at most probeCount in-flight calls. A success resets failures and returns to CLOSED; any failure reopens the circuit for another cooldown.

stopwatch.desc: Timing, intervals, and accuracy: the flip side of the countdown timer.
stopwatch.q: How will you solve this problem? Stopwatch with Lap Times
stopwatch.what:
Implement a Stopwatch class with start(), pause(), reset(), lap(), getElapsed(), and getLaps(). Track elapsed time accurately, with no drift when pausing and resuming. Expose a tick(cb) subscription for UI updates.

Requirements

  • start(): begins timing; does nothing if already running
  • pause(): stops the clock; resuming preserves the accumulated time (no drift)
  • reset(): zeroes the elapsed time and clears the laps
  • lap(): records the split time since the previous lap
  • getElapsed(): total ms since start, minus paused time
  • Accuracy: use Date.now() deltas, never a counter incremented by setInterval
  • tick(cb): calls cb(ms) periodically and returns an unsubscribe function

Concepts: Date.now() · setInterval · state machine · observer pattern
stopwatch.why:
• Track running, startTime, and accumulatedMs. On pause: accumulatedMs += now - startTime. On resume: startTime = now. elapsed = accumulatedMs + (running ? now - startTime : 0).
  • tick() runs a setInterval that calls cb(getElapsed()). For laps, snapshot {lapMs, totalMs} using the same elapsed calculation.

consistent-hashing.desc: The technique behind Redis Cluster, DynamoDB, and many distributed caches. Machine coding rounds love the ring.
consistent-hashing.q: How will you solve this problem? Consistent Hashing Ring
consistent-hashing.what:
Implement ConsistentHashing: a hash ring with N virtual nodes per server. Methods: addServer(name), removeServer(name), getServer(key). Adding or removing a server should remap only a small fraction of keys (about 1/N). Base the hash on crypto md5 or sha1.

Requirements

  • addServer(name): places vNodes virtual-node markers on the ring (default 150)
  • removeServer(name): removes all of that server's virtual-node markers
  • getServer(key): finds the first marker clockwise from the key and maps it back to its server
  • Adding or removing one server moves roughly 1/N of the keys (verify by counting remapped keys)
  • Empty ring: throw or return null (document the behavior)
  • serverStats(): per-server ownership counts for the current keys
  • getServer is deterministic for the same key

Concepts: hash ring · virtual nodes · SHA-1 · binary search · distributed systems
consistent-hashing.why:
• Ring = a sorted array of hashes plus a Map from hash to server. getServer: hash the key, binary-search for the first hash >= keyHash, and wrap around to index 0 if you go past the end.
  • Virtual nodes: for i in range(vNodes), compute hash(server + ":" + i) and place a marker that points at the server. More vNodes give a smoother distribution but use more memory.

mini-redux.desc: Implement the core Redux API from scratch, the ultimate JS architecture question.
mini-redux.q: How will you solve this problem? Build mini-Redux (createStore)

reactive.desc: Build auto-tracking reactivity, the core mechanism behind Vue 3 and MobX.
reactive.q: How will you solve this problem? Reactive Data System (Vue-like)

virtual-dom.desc: The engine inside React, Vue, and other modern frameworks. Build the core yourself.
virtual-dom.q: How will you solve this problem? Minimal Virtual DOM + Diff

observable.desc: The foundation of RxJS. Learn reactive streams by building one.
observable.q: How will you solve this problem? Build an Observable from Scratch
observable.why:
• Store the subscriber function. subscribe() creates an observer wrapper that checks an "active" flag. Operators return a new Observable: new Observable(observer => this.subscribe({next: v => observer.next(fn(v))})).
  • take(n): wrap the observer, count emissions, and call unsubscribe() when the count reaches n.

scheduler.q: How will you solve this problem? Priority Task Scheduler

di-container.q: How will you solve this problem? Dependency Injection Container
di-container.what:
Build a Container class with register(name, factory), singleton(name, factory), and resolve(name). Factory functions receive the container, so they can resolve their own dependencies. Detect circular dependencies.

Requirements

  • register: creates a new instance every time it is resolved
  • singleton: creates the instance once and caches it
  • resolve: calls the factory with the container and returns the instance
  • Detect circular dependencies and throw a descriptive error
  • Bonus: support resolving by class (auto-detect the constructor name)

Concepts: closures · Map · circular dependency detection · factory pattern

analytics-sdk.desc: The exact question Google and Atlassian ask: batching, retries, offline queueing, and session tracking.
analytics-sdk.q: How will you solve this problem? Analytics SDK (batching, retry, session)
analytics-sdk.why:
• Keep events[] in memory. flush() copies and empties the queue, then sends the batch. On failure, re-enqueue the events with a retry count and schedule a later flush.
  • Persist the whole queue as JSON on every track() (debounced). On init, load it back and flush after a short delay to recover events from an offline session.

feature-flags.desc: Every product company ships with flags. Build the SDK: rules, targeting, and deterministic bucketing.
feature-flags.q: How will you solve this problem? Feature Flag / A-B Test SDK
feature-flags.what:
Build a FeatureFlagClient. Flags are defined as {key, value, rules[]}. getFlag(key, user) evaluates the rules in order and returns the value of the first match. Support percentage rollouts (deterministic by userId hash), allowlist targeting, and conditions on user properties.

Requirements

  • getFlag(key, user): evaluates rules in order and returns the value of the first matching rule
  • Returns the default value when the flag is missing or no rule matches
  • Percentage rollout: hash(userId + key) % 100 < percent decides the bucket
  • Targeting: an allowlist of userIds and segment matching on user properties
  • Rule operators: eq, in, contains, gt, lt on user properties
  • A local overrides map for QA (overrides all rules)
  • An onEval callback fired on every evaluation, for analytics

Concepts: rules engine · deterministic hashing · user bucketing · rollout
feature-flags.why:
• hash(str): use FNV-1a or djb2 and reduce the result to 0-99. bucket = hash(userId + ":" + key). A rollout rule matches when bucket < rule.percentage.
  • Rule shape: {conditions: [{field, op, value}], percentage: 100, value}. Every condition must match AND the bucket must fall inside the percentage.

responsive-layout.q: How will you solve this problem? Responsive Dashboard Layout (CSS Grid)
responsive-layout.what:
Build a responsive dashboard layout with only HTML and CSS (no frameworks): a header, sidebar, main content area, and footer. Desktop: a fixed sidebar beside a content grid. Tablet: the sidebar collapses to icons. Mobile: a single column with a toggleable menu. Use CSS Grid for the shell and Flexbox for alignment.

Requirements

  • The header spans the full width at the top
  • The sidebar is fixed on desktop (min 220px), collapses to icons at 1024px, and hides behind a toggle at 768px
  • The main area uses CSS Grid for a card gallery that reflows from 1 to 2 to 3 columns
  • The footer sits at the bottom
  • Sticky header and sidebar that stay in view while scrolling (no scroll jump)
  • The layout works without JS; JS only drives the mobile menu toggle

Concepts: CSS Grid · Flexbox · media queries · sticky positioning
responsive-layout.why:
• Shell: display:grid; grid-template-columns: 220px 1fr; grid-template-rows: auto 1fr auto. Below 768px, switch to one column and overlay the sidebar.
  • Card gallery: grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(220px, 1fr)) reflows automatically with no media queries.

navbar-vanilla.desc: The most common CSS widget: a navbar that collapses into a hamburger menu on mobile, with no framework.
navbar-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Responsive Navbar (CSS + hamburger)
navbar-vanilla.what:
Build a responsive navbar with pure HTML/CSS and a little vanilla JS: a logo, links on the right, and active-link highlighting. Below 768px the links collapse behind a hamburger button that opens and closes the menu. Only the toggle uses JS.

Requirements

  • Logo on the left, nav links on the right on desktop
  • The active link is styled distinctly (aria-current="page")
  • Below 768px: links hidden, hamburger button shown
  • Clicking the hamburger opens and closes the mobile menu
  • Clicking a link closes the mobile menu
  • Bonus: close on the Escape key
  • No framework: pure CSS plus a class toggle

Concepts: CSS Flexbox · media queries · classList toggle · aria-expanded
navbar-vanilla.why:
• Hamburger = a button with 3 spans or an inline SVG. Rotate and translate the bars into an X when the menu is open.
  • Use aria-expanded on the button and aria-controls pointing at the menu. Escape key handler: document.addEventListener("keydown", ...).

toggle-css.q: How will you solve this problem? Custom Toggle Switch (pure CSS)
toggle-css.why:
• Wrap the input and a span: input + span. Hide the input (position:absolute; opacity:0) but keep it focusable.
  • input:checked + span: change the background and translateX() the knob. input:disabled + span: reduce the opacity.

tooltip-css.desc: A pure-CSS tooltip that stays on screen near the edges. It tests how you think about positioning.
tooltip-css.q: How will you solve this problem? Tooltip with Edge Positioning
tooltip-css.what:
Build a tooltip system that appears on hover or focus of an element. Use pure CSS positioning (top, bottom, left, or right, with an arrow), but it must clamp: a tooltip near the viewport edge must not overflow off-screen. Use data-tooltip="..." attributes so it works on any element.

Requirements

  • The tooltip shows on hover and on keyboard focus
  • Positioned above the target by default, with data-position overrides (top/bottom/left/right)
  • Near the right or bottom viewport edge, the tooltip clamps back inside the viewport
  • An arrow pointing at the target
  • A small fade/slide-in transition
  • Uses data-tooltip attributes, with no per-element JS

Concepts: position: absolute · viewport clamping · data attributes · :hover / :focus-visible
tooltip-css.why:
• Pure CSS can't know the viewport size. Position with transform and set a max-width; for true clamping, use JS to measure getBoundingClientRect() and flip the tooltip.
  • A minimal JS enhancer (document.querySelectorAll("[data-tooltip]")) can read the position and flip a class when the rect overflows.

todo-vanilla.desc: The classic widget built with no framework: DOM APIs and event delegation under pressure.
todo-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Todo App (vanilla DOM + localStorage)
todo-vanilla.what:
Build a Todo App with pure HTML/CSS/JS (no framework): add a todo on Enter, toggle completion, delete, filter All/Active/Completed, show the active count, and persist to localStorage. Edit a todo inline on double-click.

Requirements

  • Add a todo on the Enter key
  • Toggle each todo's completion
  • Delete individual todos
  • Filter tabs: All / Active / Completed
  • Show an "X items left" count
  • Persist todos to localStorage (they survive a reload)
  • Inline edit on double-click (Enter or blur to save)

Concepts: event delegation · localStorage · data-* attributes · DOM creation
todo-vanilla.why:
• Rendering approach: one render() function that rebuilds the list from state (state -> DOM). Alternatively, diff the DOM with createElement/appendChild.
  • Event delegation: one click listener on the list container, reading data-action and data-id from e.target.closest("[data-action]"). localStorage: JSON.stringify the state array on every change.

accordion-vanilla.desc: Event delegation and single/multi-open modes: the same widget as the React round, but without React.
accordion-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Accordion (vanilla)
accordion-vanilla.what:
Build an Accordion with vanilla JS: items rendered from an array [{id, title, content}], two modes (single, where one panel is open at a time, and multiple, where several can be open), a smooth max-height transition, and a chevron that rotates. No framework.

Requirements

  • Render the items from a config array
  • single mode: opening one panel closes the others
  • multiple mode: panels toggle independently
  • Smooth expand/collapse animation
  • The chevron rotates when a panel is open
  • Keyboard: Enter/Space on the header toggles it
  • aria-expanded and aria-controls wired up

Concepts: event delegation · max-height transition · aria-expanded · state flags
accordion-vanilla.why:
• Track the open ids in a Set. In single mode, opening id X sets the Set to {X}; in multiple mode, it toggles membership.
  • For the animation: set max-height from scrollHeight (panel.scrollHeight + "px") when opening, and to 0 when closing. JS measures the height; CSS animates it.

tabs-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Tabs with Keyboard Navigation
tabs-vanilla.what:
Build a Tabs component in vanilla JS: a tab list and panels. Support mouse clicks AND full keyboard navigation: Left/Right arrows move focus (roving tabindex), Home/End jump to the first or last tab, and Enter/Space activates. Wire up the ARIA roles: tablist, tab, tabpanel, and aria-selected.

Requirements

  • Clicking a tab shows its panel and hides the others
  • Left/Right arrows move between tabs (roving tabindex)
  • Home/End go to the first or last tab
  • Enter/Space activates the focused tab
  • Only the active tab is in the tab order
  • aria-selected, aria-controls, role="tablist"/"tab"/"tabpanel"
  • Panel content updates without a reload

Concepts: roving tabindex · ARIA tabs pattern · keyboard events · panel switching
tabs-vanilla.why:
• Roving tabindex: every tab has tabindex="-1" except the active one, which has tabindex="0". Arrow keys move focus and update which tab has tabindex="0".
  • Panels: render all of them in the DOM and toggle the hidden attribute. aria-selected must be set on the tab button.

modal-vanilla.desc: Focus trap, scroll lock, Escape handling: the hardest "easy" widget without React's portal.
modal-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Modal with Focus Trap (no portal)
modal-vanilla.what:
Build a Modal dialog in vanilla JS (no React, no portal): open it on a button click, show an overlay with a centered dialog, and close on Escape, on an overlay click, and on the X button. Trap focus inside while it is open, restore focus to the trigger on close, and lock body scroll.

Requirements

  • Open and close with a smooth fade
  • Close via Escape, overlay click, and the X button
  • Focus moves into the dialog on open
  • Tab/Shift+Tab cycle inside the dialog (focus trap)
  • Focus returns to the trigger button on close
  • Body scroll is locked while open (overflow:hidden)
  • role="dialog", aria-modal="true", aria-labelledby

Concepts: focus trap · event listeners · overflow lock · ARIA dialog
modal-vanilla.why:
• Focus trap: add a keydown listener. If e.key === "Tab", collect the focusable elements in the dialog and wrap the index at the ends. Save document.activeElement before opening.
  • Escape: use a document keydown listener, and remove all listeners on close to avoid leaks. Overlay click: check e.target === overlay.

star-rating-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Star Rating (event delegation)
star-rating-vanilla.what:
Build a star rating widget: 5 stars, where hovering highlights up to the hovered star, clicking sets the rating, and moving the mouse out restores the chosen rating. Support the keyboard (arrow keys change the value) and a reset. Render from JS.

Requirements

  • Renders 5 interactive stars
  • Hover previews the rating without committing it
  • Click commits the rating
  • Mouse leave restores the committed rating
  • Keyboard: arrow keys adjust, Enter commits
  • Programmatic API: setRating(n) / getRating()
  • Empty and filled star glyphs switch smoothly

Concepts: event delegation · mouseover/mouseout · keydown · re-render
star-rating-vanilla.why:
• Put one listener on the container. e.target.closest(".star") gives the star, and a data-rating attribute on each star gives its index.
  • Keep state = {hovered, value}. render() redraws the star classes: a star is filled when i <= (hovered || value).

stopwatch-vanilla.desc: setInterval drift and lap recording: precise timing under the microscope.
stopwatch-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Stopwatch with Laps
stopwatch-vanilla.what:
Build a stopwatch in vanilla JS with Start/Pause/Reset buttons, an elapsed-time display (MM:SS.cs), and a lap list that records each lap's cumulative time and its delta from the previous lap. Base the timer on timestamps so it never drifts.

Requirements

  • Start, Pause and Reset controls
  • Display updates with centisecond precision
  • Uses timestamps (performance.now()), not interval counting
  • Lap button records the cumulative time and the lap delta
  • Laps render as a scrollable list, newest first
  • Reset clears the laps and the display
  • Format: MM:SS.cc

Concepts: setInterval vs timestamps · performance.now() · state machine · DOM list rendering
stopwatch-vanilla.why:
• Drift fix: save startTime when the timer starts. On each tick, compute elapsed = accumulated + (now - startTime). The interval only triggers a re-render, roughly every 50ms.
  • Lap delta = current elapsed - elapsed at the previous lap. Store laps as [{cum, delta}], build the rows in a fragment, and prepend it to the list.

countdown-vanilla.desc: A ring that drains as time passes: SVG stroke-dashoffset meets the timer pattern.
countdown-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Countdown Timer with Progress Ring
countdown-vanilla.what:
Build a countdown timer with an SVG progress ring. The user sets minutes and seconds, starts, pauses or resets, and the ring visibly drains as time runs out. In the last 10 seconds, flash the display red, and trigger an alarm state at zero. Preset buttons (1/5/10 min) are optional.

Requirements

  • Set the target duration (minutes and seconds inputs)
  • Start, Pause and Reset
  • The SVG ring drains in proportion to elapsed time
  • Display shows remaining time as MM:SS
  • Last 10s: the number turns red or pulses
  • At zero: stop, show 00:00 and a visual alarm
  • Runs from a deadline timestamp, not by decrementing a counter

Concepts: SVG stroke-dashoffset · deadline timestamps · requestAnimationFrame/setInterval · state machine
countdown-vanilla.why:
• Ring: draw a circle with stroke-dasharray = C (the circumference) and stroke-dashoffset = C * (1 - remaining/total). Add a transition on the offset for smooth motion.
  • Deadline: store end = Date.now() + remainingMs. On each tick, compute remainingMs = end - Date.now(). This is immune to setInterval drift and background-tab throttling.

form-validation-vanilla.desc: Real-time validation with error messages and accessibility: the form round nobody practices.
form-validation-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Inline Form Validation
form-validation-vanilla.what:
Build a form (name, email, password, confirm password) with vanilla JS validation. Validate on blur and on submit, show inline error messages, mark invalid fields with an error style and aria-invalid, focus the first invalid field on submit, and clear each error as the user types.

Requirements

  • Rules: name is non-empty, email matches a regex, password is at least 8 characters with a number, confirmation matches
  • Errors appear inline under each field
  • Validate on blur and on submit
  • Invalid fields get an .error class and aria-invalid=true
  • On submit: focus the first invalid field and don't send
  • Each error clears as the user fixes the input
  • A success message appears when valid; no framework

Concepts: FormData · regex validation · blur/submit/input events · aria-invalid
form-validation-vanilla.why:
• Map each field to a validator function that returns an error string, or "" when valid. A single validateField(el) function reads that map.
  • On submit, run every validator, collect the invalid fields, focus the first one, and call e.preventDefault(). For better UX, validate a field only after it has been touched (blurred once).

carousel-vanilla.desc: Infinite looping, dots, swipe and auto-play: the widget that is 90% edge cases.
carousel-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Image Carousel (vanilla)
carousel-vanilla.what:
Build an image carousel in vanilla JS with prev/next arrows, dot indicators, auto-play that pauses on hover, and a wrapping loop (the first slide follows the last). Support touch swipe on mobile. No framework.

Requirements

  • Prev/next arrows advance and wrap around
  • Dot indicators show the current slide and jump to any slide
  • Auto-play every 3s; stops on hover or focus and resumes on leave
  • Swipe left/right on touch devices
  • Animated slide transition (translateX)
  • A slide counter or aria-live region for accessibility
  • Resizes gracefully with no layout jump

Concepts: translateX transforms · setInterval auto-play · touch events · indices with modulo

infinite-scroll-vanilla.desc: A sentinel element plus IntersectionObserver loads the next page: async UX fundamentals.
infinite-scroll-vanilla.q: How would you solve this problem? Infinite Scroll (IntersectionObserver)
infinite-scroll-vanilla.what:
Build an infinite scroll list in vanilla JS. Start with 20 items; when the user scrolls to the sentinel element, fetch and render the next 20 with a loading spinner, and make sure it can't double-fire. Show "no more" at the end. Items can come from a mock async source.

Requirements

  • Renders the initial batch of items
  • Loads more when the sentinel enters the viewport
  • Uses IntersectionObserver, not scroll math
  • Spinner shows while loading; no duplicate loads
  • Stops loading once there are no more items
  • New items append without layout thrash
  • Optionally batch DOM updates with requestAnimationFrame

Concepts: IntersectionObserver · async data source · sentinel pattern · lazy rendering
infinite-scroll-vanilla.why:
• Place an empty div at the bottom of the list and call observer.observe(sentinel). In the callback, load more if isIntersecting and nothing is loading.
  • Guard: check a loading flag before fetching and reset it in finally. When the source is exhausted, unobserve the sentinel.

autocomplete-vanilla.desc: The canonical frontend problem without React: async, debounce, keyboard navigation, highlighting.
autocomplete-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Autocomplete (debounce + keyboard)
autocomplete-vanilla.what:
Build a production-quality autocomplete in vanilla JS: a text input, debounced suggestions (300ms) from a mock async API, a dropdown filtered on the client, Up/Down/Enter/Escape keyboard navigation, and highlighted matching substrings. Handle loading and empty states.

Requirements

  • Debounce the suggestion request by 300ms
  • Show a loading indicator while waiting for results
  • Keyboard: Up/Down move the highlight, Enter selects, Escape closes
  • Highlight the matching text inside each suggestion
  • Clicking selects a suggestion
  • Show an empty-results state
  • Cache results by query string

Concepts: debounce · async/await · keyboard navigation · highlighting matches
autocomplete-vanilla.why:
• Debounce: call clearTimeout/setTimeout in the input's "input" handler. Cache: a Map.
  • Highlight: for each suggestion, find the query's index and wrap the match in (or a span.highlight). Escape the HTML in the server text first.

pagination-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Client-side Pagination
pagination-vanilla.what:
Build a pagination control in vanilla JS for a fixed data array: N items per page, prev/next buttons, page-number buttons with a sliding window (current page in the middle, ellipses at the edges), and a "Showing X–Y of Z" line. Render the list from the current slice.

Requirements

  • Configurable page size (e.g. 10)
  • Prev/Next buttons, disabled at the ends
  • Page-number buttons with a sliding window and ellipses
  • Active page highlighted and marked aria-current="page"
  • The "Showing X–Y of Z" caption updates
  • Clicking a number re-renders only the list and controls
  • Handles the edge case of fewer items than one page

Concepts: slice() pagination · windowed page lists · ellipsis logic · re-rendering
pagination-vanilla.why:
• currentSlice = data.slice((page-1)*size, page*size). Re-render the list and caption on every page change.
  • Page window: show at most 7 numbers, laid out as 1 … left neighbors … current … right neighbors … last, with "…" wherever there's a gap. Build the array conditionally.

traffic-light-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Traffic Light State Machine
traffic-light-vanilla.what:
Build a traffic light with vanilla JS: three circles (red/amber/green). A finite state machine cycles through them automatically (red 4s → amber 1s → green 3s → amber 1s → red). Clicking the light advances one state manually, which is handy for testing.

Requirements

  • Three lamp circles, one active at a time
  • Automatic cycle with a duration per state
  • Manual advance on click (moves to the next state)
  • Model it as an explicit state machine, not scattered if/else
  • Start immediately on load
  • Clear transition between states

Concepts: state machines · setTimeout chains · state -> view mapping · event-driven updates
traffic-light-vanilla.why:
• Define states = [{id:"red",next:"amber",ms:4000}, ...]. A setState(s) function renders the light and schedules a setTimeout for the next state.
  • Keep the timer handle so a manual click can call clearTimeout and jump ahead. A manual advance uses the same next pointer.

grid-light-vanilla.desc: A classic Flipkart machine coding round: click a cell, light up its diagonal, then reset in order.
grid-light-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Grid Light (Flipkart round)
grid-light-vanilla.what:
Build a Grid Light (Flipkart-style): a 3x3 grid. Clicking a cell turns it on along with its diagonal cells. When all 9 cells are on, they turn off one by one in the order they were activated. Track the activation order explicitly.

Requirements

  • 3x3 grid rendered from JS
  • Clicking a cell lights it and its diagonal cells
  • Cells follow the diagonal rule rather than toggling independently
  • When all cells are on, they turn off sequentially in activation order
  • Lighting respects the diagonal dependency
  • Restarts cleanly after the reset sequence

Concepts: state tracking · activation order · grid modeling · async timing
grid-light-vanilla.why:
• Model the diagonal mapping as [[0,0],[1,1],[2,2]]. A cell(i,j) is on if any clicked cell on its diagonal lit it, so derive the state from the set of clicked cells instead of mutating flags.
  • For the reset, keep an order[] of clicked cells. When the grid is full, run a setTimeout chain that turns cells off in that order with a small delay.

tic-tac-toe-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Tic-Tac-Toe with History (vanilla)
tic-tac-toe-vanilla.what:
Build Tic-Tac-Toe in vanilla JS: two players alternate X and O, with win detection for rows, columns and diagonals, a draw state, a status line, and a move history that lets you jump back to any earlier board. No framework.

Requirements

  • Clicking an empty cell places the current player's mark
  • Turns alternate between X and O
  • Wins detected for 3 rows, 3 columns and 2 diagonals
  • Draw detected when the board is full with no winner
  • Status line shows whose turn it is, or the result
  • Move history lists every move; clicking one jumps to that state
  • Past states are immutable (no mutation bugs)

Concepts: game state modeling · win detection · immutable snapshots · history navigation
tic-tac-toe-vanilla.why:
• Represent the board as an array of 9. For the win check, test the 8 winning triples with Array.every. Each move pushes a copy of the board into history.
  • History jump: slice the history array and rebuild the board from the chosen index. Never mutate past boards in place.

memory-game-vanilla.q: How would you solve this problem? Memory Match Game
memory-game-vanilla.why:
• Shuffle with Fisher-Yates: for i from n-1 down to 1, swap with a random index in 0..i. Store cards as {id, value}.
  • State: flipped holds up to 2 card ids, plus a Set of matched ids. On the second flip, compare values. If they match, add them to matched; otherwise use setTimeout (800ms) to flip both back, and lock clicks during the wait.

calculator-vanilla.desc: Operator precedence, chained math and display state: the trickiest "simple" UI.
calculator-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Calculator
calculator-vanilla.what:
Build a calculator in vanilla JS with digits 0-9, a decimal point, + - × ÷, clear, and equals. Support chained operations (2 + 3 × 4 = 14) with correct operator precedence, and prevent double operators and leading zeros. Support keyboard input (digits and operators).

Requirements

  • Digit and decimal input with sensible limits
  • +, -, ×, ÷ with precedence (×/÷ before +/-)
  • Chained evaluation, e.g. 2 + 3 × 4 = 14
  • Equals computes the result and lets you continue from it
  • Clear resets; backspace deletes the last digit
  • Handles divide-by-zero gracefully
  • Keyboard support for digits, operators and Enter

Concepts: tokenization · operator precedence · display state · keyboard events
calculator-vanilla.why:
• Build the expression as tokens and evaluate it with shunting-yard, or in two passes: first × and ÷, then + and - (left to right).
  • Keep the display as the current number string and build a separate expression string for evaluation. Guards: a leading "." becomes "0.", no "..", and no trailing operator when equals is pressed.

weather-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Weather App (fetch + states)
weather-vanilla.why:
• State machine: {status: idle|loading|success|error|notfound, data}. render() switches on status, giving one render path per state.
  • Mock API: a function that returns a Promise resolving after a delay with a fake forecast map keyed by city. Simulate an error by having the same function reject for an unknown city, and debounce the search input.

file-upload-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Drag & Drop File Upload
file-upload-vanilla.what:
Build a file upload zone in vanilla JS: a drop area (highlighted on drag-over), a file input fallback, a file list showing name and size, image previews, and simulated upload progress bars with cancel. Restrict to images (or use an accept filter).

Requirements

  • Click-to-browse opens the file picker
  • Drag-over highlights the drop zone
  • Dropping adds files to the list (no duplicates)
  • Image previews rendered via URL.createObjectURL
  • Each file shows its name, size and a progress bar
  • Simulated upload with progress and cancel
  • An invalid type shows an error toast

Concepts: dragenter/dragover/drop · URL.createObjectURL · progress simulation · file validation
file-upload-vanilla.why:
• Call preventDefault on dragover and drop, or the browser will navigate away to the file. Track a drag counter to avoid flicker when the pointer enters and leaves child elements.
  • Progress: use setInterval to advance 0->100 per file, or a slow-approach curve (p += (100-p)*0.1). Cancel = clearInterval and mark the file as failed.

drag-drop-vanilla.desc: HTML5 drag and drop with live reordering: the interview favorite that trips everyone up.
drag-drop-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Drag & Drop Reorder / Kanban
drag-drop-vanilla.what:
Build a drag-and-drop list (or single-column kanban) in vanilla JS: drag items to reorder them, with a live insertion indicator (ghost) showing where the item will land. Handle dragstart, dragover and drop, and re-render the list from state after every drop.

Requirements

  • Drag an item to reorder it within the list
  • Live visual insertion point while dragging
  • Dropping commits the new order (state updates)
  • Only the dragged item moves, not a copy
  • Drag handle or full-row draggable
  • Keyboard alternative for reordering (bonus)
  • Mouse-only is fine (touch is a bonus)

Concepts: dragstart/dragover/drop · dragenter index math · state-based re-rendering · visual feedback
drag-drop-vanilla.why:
• On dragover, compute the target index from the list items' bounding boxes and show a ghost line before or after that item.
  • On drop, splice the dragged item out of state and back in at the ghost index, then re-render the list. The source item keeps the dragging class for the duration of the drag.

toast-vanilla.desc: A queue, auto-dismiss and stacking: the tiny system that separates widget coders from system builders.
toast-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Toast Notification System
toast-vanilla.what:
Build a toast notification system in vanilla JS with a toast(message, type) API (success/info/error/warning). Toasts stack in the top-right, auto-dismiss after 4s, have a manual close button, and never overlap. Cap the visible stack (e.g. at 5).

Requirements

  • toast(message, type) is the public API
  • Four types with distinct colors and icons
  • Auto-dismiss after 4s, with a countdown (bonus)
  • Manual close button
  • Toasts stack cleanly in a top-right container
  • Max 5 visible; the oldest is removed beyond that
  • Accessibility: role="status" or "alert" on each toast

Concepts: event emitter / pub-sub · DOM creation · timers · container pattern
toast-vanilla.why:
• Create one fixed, top-right container div on init. Each toast is a div appended to it with a class per type.
  • Auto-dismiss: setTimeout(remove, 4000). To enforce the max of N, remove the first child when the length exceeds 5. The close button removes the toast and clears its timer.

chips-input-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Chips / Tags Input
chips-input-vanilla.what:
Build a chips (tags) input in vanilla JS: type a tag and press Enter (or comma) to add it as a chip. Each chip has an × to remove it, pressing Backspace on an empty input removes the last chip, and duplicates are rejected with a shake or error flash. Provide a getter for the chips.

Requirements

  • Enter or comma commits the typed value as a chip
  • Chips render with a remove (×) button
  • Backspace on an empty input removes the last chip
  • Duplicates are rejected with an error flash
  • Leading and trailing whitespace is trimmed
  • The input clears after a chip is committed
  • Chips are accessible: getChips() returns the array

Concepts: keydown handling · deduplication · chip removal · input width auto-grow
chips-input-vanilla.why:
• Handle keydown on the input: Enter or comma commits; Backspace with value=="" removes the last chip; Escape clears the input.
  • Auto-grow the input: set its width from scrollWidth (or from a hidden mirror span) so the text never overflows the chip row.

snake-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Snake on Canvas
snake-vanilla.what:
Build Snake on a <canvas> with vanilla JS: a grid-based snake that moves on a fixed tick, grows when it eats food, and either wraps or dies at the walls (your choice, so state it up front). It dies on self-collision and has a score and restart. Support arrow/WASD input with direction buffering so a fast turn isn't lost.

Requirements

  • Snake moves on a fixed interval (grid tick)
  • Arrow keys and WASD control direction
  • The snake can't reverse into itself
  • Input buffering: two rapid turns within one tick both register
  • Food spawns at a random empty cell
  • Eating grows the snake and increments the score
  • Self-collision ends the game; a restart button resets it
  • Rendered on canvas with a clear frame loop

Concepts: game loop · linked-list / queue body model · input buffering · canvas rendering
snake-vanilla.why:
• Model the snake as a queue with the head at the front. To move, unshift(newHead) and pop the tail (unless the snake is growing). To render the body, draw a rect for each cell.
  • Input buffer: push direction changes into an array. On each tick, shift one off and apply it only if it isn't the reverse of the current direction.

minesweeper-vanilla.desc: Flood-fill reveal, adjacency counting and chording: a Google favorite for hard rounds.
minesweeper-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Minesweeper (flood fill)
minesweeper-vanilla.what:
Build Minesweeper in vanilla JS: a 9x9 board with 10 mines, a safe first click, and cells that reveal an adjacent-mine count. Zero cells flood-fill open (BFS/DFS), right-click flags a cell, you win when all non-mine cells are revealed, and you lose on clicking a mine. Include a timer and reset.

Requirements

  • 9x9 grid with 10 randomly placed mines
  • The first click never hits a mine (relocate it if needed)
  • Revealing a 0 opens its whole region (flood fill)
  • Numbers show adjacent mine counts
  • Right-click flags or unflags a cell (with a counter)
  • Clicking a mine reveals everything and ends the game
  • Win is detected when every non-mine cell is revealed
  • Reset reshuffles and restarts

Concepts: flood fill (BFS) · adjacency counting · game state · right-click handling
minesweeper-vanilla.why:
• Model the board as a 2D array of cell objects {mine, revealed, flagged, adj}. For the flood fill, use a BFS queue (or DFS stack): push in-bounds neighbors of revealed 0-cells, skipping visited ones.
  • Place the mines after the first click, picking from a candidate list that excludes the clicked cell and its neighbors. adj = the number of mines among the 8 neighbors.

game-2048-vanilla.desc: Tile merging, sliding and spawn logic: the ultimate grid state-machine round.
game-2048-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? 2048 Game
game-2048-vanilla.what:
Build the 2048 game in vanilla JS: a 4x4 grid where arrow keys slide all tiles in that direction, equal adjacent tiles merge (each tile merges at most once per move), and a random 2 or 4 spawns after each valid move. The score tracks merged values, and the game ends when no moves remain (or 2048 is reached).

Requirements

  • Arrow keys slide and merge all tiles
  • A tile merges at most once per move
  • A random 2 (90%) or 4 (10%) spawns after a valid move
  • A move that changes nothing leaves the board unchanged
  • Score increases by the merged values
  • Win banner at 2048 (continuing is optional)
  • Game over when the board is full and no merges are possible
  • Animated slide and merge feel (CSS transitions)

Concepts: grid transformation · merge logic · spawn logic · valid-move detection
game-2048-vanilla.why:
• Slide-left algorithm: for each row, compress (remove zeros), merge adjacent equal tiles once, then compress again. Rotate the board to reuse this one routine for all four directions.
  • A move is valid only if some cell changed, so copy the board before the attempt (JSON or structuredClone) and compare. To check whether any move is possible, look for an empty cell or any adjacent equal pair.

canvas-drawing-vanilla.q: How would you solve this problem? Drawing Board with Undo/Redo
canvas-drawing-vanilla.what:
Build a drawing board on canvas: draw freehand with a mouse or pen (pointer events), pick a color and stroke width, undo/redo stroke by stroke, and clear. Store the history as stroke arrays (not pixel images) so undo is cheap and lossless.

Requirements

  • Freehand drawing via pointer events (down/move/up)
  • Color and stroke-width pickers apply live
  • Undo removes the last stroke; redo restores it
  • Clear wipes the board
  • Stroke model: [{points, color, width}]
  • High-DPI aware: size the canvas using devicePixelRatio
  • Touch support (pointer events unify mouse and touch)

Concepts: Pointer Events · stroke vectorization · undo/redo stacks · canvas DPI scaling

virtual-list-vanilla.desc: Render 100,000 rows with about 10 DOM nodes: the performance round everyone flubs.
virtual-list-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Virtual Scrolling List
virtual-list-vanilla.what:
Build a virtual scrolling list in vanilla JS: render only the visible window of a large array (e.g. 100,000 rows) inside a fixed-height scroll container. On scroll, compute the visible range, render only those rows using absolute or translateY positioning, and keep a small buffer. Variable row heights are an optional bonus.

Requirements

  • Fixed-height scroll container
  • Renders only the visible rows plus a buffer (e.g. 5 on each side)
  • Row positions use translateY, not top (no layout thrash)
  • Handles 100k+ rows without lag
  • Scroll position stays stable when jumping to a row
  • Clicking a row fires a callback with the row index
  • Resizing or changing row height triggers re-measurement

Concepts: virtualization · scroll events + rAF throttling · translateY positioning · range math

data-table-vanilla.desc: Sorting, filtering and row selection: the most common dashboard component.
data-table-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Sortable / Filterable Data Table

chat-vanilla.desc: A WebSocket client, message list and reconnect logic: real-time from the raw API.
chat-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? WebSocket Chat UI (vanilla)
chat-vanilla.what:
Build a chat UI in vanilla JS that talks to a WebSocket endpoint: send messages, render incoming ones (own vs. other with different alignment), show a typing indicator and online status, auto-scroll to the latest message, and reconnect with backoff after a disconnect. Include a message input that sends on Enter.

Requirements

  • Connects to a WebSocket (ws:// or a mock)
  • Send a message via the input with Enter or a button
  • Renders own and peer messages with different alignment
  • Auto-scrolls to the newest message unless the user has scrolled up
  • Online/disconnected status indicator
  • Reconnects with exponential backoff
  • Typing indicator (bonus)
  • Handles connection errors gracefully

Concepts: WebSocket API · reconnect backoff · message rendering · scroll anchoring
chat-vanilla.why:
• Socket events: onopen, onmessage, onclose, onerror. Reflect the connection state in a status banner. To reconnect, schedule ws = new WebSocket(url) with an increasing delay, and reset the delay on open.
  • Scroll anchoring: if the user is near the bottom (scrollTop close to the max), auto-scroll after appending. Otherwise, show a "new message" jump chip.

reactive-framework-vanilla.desc: Reactive state -> DOM updates: the tiny framework behind Vue and Solid, built by hand.
reactive-framework-vanilla.q: How would you solve this problem? Mini Reactive DOM Framework

dom-diff-vanilla.desc: createElement, mount and patch: build the core of React's reconciliation in vanilla JS.
dom-diff-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Virtual DOM Diff (vanilla)

spreadsheet-vanilla.desc: A grid of cells, formula evaluation and dependency recalculation: the wildcard round.
spreadsheet-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Spreadsheet Grid with Formulas
spreadsheet-vanilla.why:
• Parse cell references with a regex like ([A-J])(\d+). Build a dependency graph (cell -> dependents). On an edit, recompute the affected cells in topological order.
  • Evaluate safely. Substituting referenced values into the expression and running it through new Function(...) works but is unsafe. Better: write a tiny recursive-descent evaluator that handles + - * / and SUM/AVG over ranges.

file-explorer-vanilla.desc: A recursive folder tree with expand/collapse, CRUD and rename: recursion in the DOM.
file-explorer-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? File Explorer (Folder Tree)
file-explorer-vanilla.what:
Build a file explorer in vanilla JS from a nested {name, type: 'folder'|'file', children?} tree. Render the hierarchy recursively, let folders expand and collapse with an arrow, select files on click, and offer toolbar actions (new folder, new file, rename, delete) on the selected node. Handle empty folders, deep nesting and indentation guides.

Requirements

  • Renders the full tree recursively (folders containing files and folders)
  • The folder arrow toggles expand/collapse; the state persists
  • Clicking selects a node (highlight and enable the toolbar)
  • New folder / new file creates a child under the selected folder
  • Rename edits the node name inline (Enter/Escape)
  • Delete removes the node and its whole subtree
  • Handles long folder names and deep paths
  • Indentation guides render for each depth level

Concepts: recursive rendering · tree CRUD · immutable tree updates · event delegation
file-explorer-vanilla.why:
• Keep the state as a single tree object, and have every operation return a new tree (recursively mapping over children). Write one recursive renderNode(node, depth) function and compose containers from it.
  • Delegation: one click listener reads data-id, resolves the node's path, then re-renders. Store a path array (of indices) in data-path so operations can rebuild the tree immutably.

nested-comments-vanilla.desc: Recursive comment threads with reply, delete and voting: the infinite-nesting classic.
nested-comments-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Nested Comments (Reddit-style)
nested-comments-vanilla.what:
Build nested comments in vanilla JS: a top-level comment box, with replies that nest recursively to any depth. Each comment has reply, upvote/downvote and delete (with a confirmation). Reply opens an inline editor, and every comment shows an author, a relative time and a score. A collapse toggle hides a comment and all of its children.

Requirements

  • Comments render as a recursive thread tree
  • Reply adds a child comment at any depth
  • Inline reply editor (textarea with post/cancel)
  • Upvote/downvote changes the score (one vote per comment)
  • Delete removes the comment and all its descendants
  • Collapse toggle hides a comment and its subtree
  • Authors and relative timestamps are shown
  • No framework: plain DOM building and event delegation

Concepts: recursive rendering · tree state updates · event delegation · voting state
nested-comments-vanilla.why:
• A comment node is {id, author, text, time, score, children[]}. renderThread(comment) returns the DOM for that subtree. Re-render the whole thread after every mutation, since the data is small.
  • Reply: keep editingCommentId in state, and render the editor inline under that node. Delete: filter the node out recursively by mapping over children.

json-tree-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? JSON Tree Viewer
json-tree-vanilla.what:
Build a JSON tree viewer in vanilla JS: paste any JSON (or load a sample) and render it as an indented, collapsible tree. Objects and arrays expand and collapse with a toggle, primitives are color-coded (string green, number blue, boolean purple, null gray), clicking a key copies its path, and a search box highlights matching keys and jumps to the first one.

Requirements

  • Parses JSON input (shows an error state for invalid JSON)
  • Objects and arrays render with expand/collapse toggles
  • Type-based color coding for primitives
  • Clicking a key copies its JSONPath (e.g. a.b[0].c)
  • Search highlights matching keys and jumps to the first
  • Large inputs stay responsive (render children lazily)
  • Empty objects and arrays show inline as {} / []

Concepts: recursive rendering · mixed-type introspection · JSONPath · lazy expansion

checkbox-tree-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Cascading Checkbox Tree
checkbox-tree-vanilla.what:
Build a cascading checkbox tree in vanilla JS from a nested permissions list (e.g. Settings > Notifications > Email). Checking a parent checks all its descendants, unchecking clears them all, a partially checked parent shows an indeterminate box, and any manual change to a child recomputes its ancestors. A footer shows selected / total counts.

Requirements

  • Renders a nested checkbox list recursively
  • Checking a parent checks its entire subtree
  • Unchecking a parent unchecks its entire subtree
  • A parent with some checked children shows the indeterminate state
  • Toggling a child manually recomputes all its ancestors
  • The footer shows the leaf count and the selected count
  • Clicking the checkbox or its label both toggle the node

Concepts: recursive state propagation · indeterminate state · derived state · tree traversal

directory-size-vanilla.desc: Recursive size aggregation over a fake filesystem: the math behind disk-usage tools.
directory-size-vanilla.q: How will you solve this problem? Directory Size Calculator
directory-size-vanilla.what:
Build a directory size calculator in vanilla JS: a fake file tree where files carry byte sizes and folders aggregate the total of their subtree, rendered with each node's size right-aligned. Expand and collapse folders, sort children by size in descending order, and add a "calculate all" scan that animates the folder totals filling in (walking the tree recursively with a delay).

Requirements

  • File tree with per-file sizes and folders that aggregate their subtrees
  • Size shown right-aligned on each row, formatted (B/KB/MB)
  • Expand/collapse folders
  • Sort children by size, descending (toggle)
  • Scan animation: folder totals fill in bottom-up
  • Recursive aggregation computes each total once and caches it
  • For large trees, the total is displayed at the root

Concepts: recursive aggregation · post-order traversal · size formatting · animation timing
directory-size-vanilla.why:
• A folder's size is the sum of its children, computed in post-order: size(node) = sum of file sizes + folders.map(size). Cache the results in a Map so toggling the sort doesn't recompute anything.
  • For the scan animation, flatten the post-order sequence into a list, then reveal each folder's total on a setTimeout/setInterval tick (or with rAF).
